description: Width tiers for Year 2 Science — ACARA v9. Covers the three U-strand descriptors. H-strand and I-strand (1–2 band) are in science_y1_2_width_tiers.json.
subject: Science

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest floor — fewest phenomena or contexts that still genuinely satisfy the descriptor.
width_notes.typical_width: Full scope grounded in the most common elaboration cases.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions adding phenomena, cultural contexts or applications. First Nations directions included where elaborations indicate them.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations treated as source data. Typical grounded in common cases.

AC9S2U01.minimum_width: Name Earth as a planet in the solar system and identify at least two other planets; describe the pattern of the sun's movement across a day; describe at least two moon phases and make one prediction based on the monthly pattern.
AC9S2U01.typical_width: Explore solar system representations; describe Earth's shape from space images; distinguish day and night sky objects; identify patterns in sun position and shadow length across a day; create a moon diary across a month identifying pattern and making predictions; observe and describe short-term and longer-term sky patterns.
wider: Explore how cultural stories of First Nations Peoples of Australia describe patterns in the sun, moon and stars — comparing knowledge frameworks
Create a class model of the solar system naming the sun and planets
Distinguish regular sky events (full moon) from irregular events (blood moon, blue moon)
View time-lapse video of sun, moon, stars or satellite movement — using digital tools to observe patterns invisible at normal timescales
elaborations: identifying celestial objects visible in space: sun, moon, stars, planets
viewing images or video of Earth from space and describing Earth's shape
exploring representations of the solar system and identifying Earth and other planets
observing day and night sky phenomena
investigating how shadow length changes with changing sun position
creating a class moon diary across a month identifying patterns and making predictions
observing short-term and longer-term sky patterns
distinguishing regular and irregular sky events
exploring First Nations cultural stories about patterns in the sun, moon and stars

AC9S2U02.minimum_width: Name at least four different sound-producing actions with examples; describe vibrations in one sound-making object and explain that the object vibrates because of sound energy.
AC9S2U02.typical_width: Explore and classify instruments by sound-producing action (striking, blowing, plucking, scraping, shaking); describe how traditional First Nations instruments produce sound; observe vibrations from a ruler, tuning fork or speaker; connect vibration speed/strength to loudness and pitch; design and make a simple instrument.
wider: Explore how traditional musical instruments used by First Nations Australians produce their characteristic sounds
Investigate which materials best muffle sound — examining how materials absorb or block vibrations
Discuss echolocation in dolphins and bats — connecting sound vibration to animal navigation
Explore how music can be understood as patterns of sounds (AC9S2H01)
elaborations: building vocabulary for loudness and pitch, comparing instrument sounds
exploring different ways to produce sound using familiar objects and actions
exploring traditional First Nations Australian instruments
observing vibrations from a twanged ruler
investigating how sound energy makes things vibrate
investigating which materials muffle sound
designing and making instruments
discussing echolocation in humans with vision impairment and other animals

AC9S2U03.minimum_width: Apply at least two physical changes to a material and name each action; explain that the material is still the same substance after the change; compare how the same action affects two different materials.
AC9S2U03.typical_width: Manipulate multiple materials with multiple actions (scrunching, twisting, bending, cutting, tearing, folding, crushing); explain that physical changes alter shape but not composition; describe purposeful physical changes; compare properties of original and changed material.
wider: Crush chalk into powder and discuss whether it is still the same material — challenging composition understanding
Explore how First Nations Australians make physical changes to natural materials to produce bowls, baskets and fibre crafts
Create an 'odd one out' game using physically changed vs different materials — applying composition knowledge to classification
Learn from material workers (woodworkers, fibre artists, sculptors) about how they manipulate material properties (AC9S2H01)
elaborations: exploring how materials can be physically changed for particular purposes
manipulating paper, fabric and other materials through multiple physical changes
crushing chalk and comparing properties of stick vs powder
exploring how First Nations Australians make physical changes to natural materials
creating an 'odd one out' game using same-material physical changes
